content: Azithromycin has been studied for its tissue and fluid concentrations in various body sites, including bone, ejaculate, prostate, ovary, uterus, fallopian tubes, stomach, liver, and gallbladder. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled clinical studies evaluating the efficacy of azithromycin in treating infections at these specific sites. Consequently, the clinical significance of the tissue concentration data remains unknown. Pharmacokinetics Following a Single Dose: After a single oral dose of 1200 mg (administered as two 600 mg tablets), the mean maximum concentration of azithromycin in peripheral leukocytes was 140 µg/mL. Concentrations remained above 32 µg/mL for approximately 60 hours. The mean half-life was 34 hours in males and 57 hours in females. The leukocyte-to-plasma Cmax ratios were 258 (±77%) in males and 175 (±60%) in females, while the AUC ratios were 804 (±31%) and 541 (±28%) in males and females, respectively. The clinical relevance of these findings is not established. Pharmacokinetics Following Multiple Doses: In asymptomatic HIV-positive adults receiving daily doses of 600 mg (one tablet per day), the mean maximum concentration in peripheral leukocytes was 252 µg/mL (±49%). At steady state, the mean trough concentration in leukocytes was 146 µg/mL (±33%). The mean leukocyte-to-serum Cmax ratio was 456 (±38%), and the mean leukocyte-to-serum AUC ratio was 816 (±31%). Metabolism: No in vitro or in vivo studies have been conducted to evaluate the metabolism of azithromycin. Elimination: Plasma concentrations of azithromycin following a single 500 mg oral or intravenous dose declined in a multiphasic pattern, resulting in an average terminal half-life of 68 hours. Biliary excretion, primarily as unchanged drug, is the major route of elimination. Approximately 6% of the administered dose is excreted unchanged in the urine over the course of a week. Specific Populations: Renal Insufficiency: Azithromycin pharmacokinetics were studied in 42 adults aged 21 to 85 years with varying degrees of renal impairment. In subjects with a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 10 to 80 mL/min, the mean Cmax and AUC0–120 increased by 61% and 35%, respectively, compared to subjects with normal renal function (GFR >80 mL/min). In end-stage renal disease, the mean Cmax and AUC0–120 increased by 61% and 35%, respectively. Hepatic Insufficiency: The pharmacokinetics of azithromycin in individuals with hepatic impairment have not been established. Gender: There are no significant differences in the pharmacokinetics of azithromycin between male and female subjects. No dosage adjustment is recommended based on gender. Geriatric Patients: Pharmacokinetic parameters in older adults (65 to 85 years) were similar to those in younger adults (18 to 40 years) for the 5-day therapeutic regimen. Dosage adjustment does not appear necessary for older patients with normal renal and hepatic function. Pediatric Patients: For information on the pharmacokinetics of azithromycin in pediatric patients, refer to the prescribing information for ZITHROMAX oral suspension (100 mg/5 mL and 200 mg/5 mL bottles). Drug-Drug Interactions: Drug interaction studies have been conducted with azithromycin and other drugs likely to be co-administered. Co-administration of azithromycin at therapeutic doses had a modest effect on the pharmacokinetics of the drugs listed in the studies. No dosage adjustment of these drugs is recommended when co-administered with azithromycin. Co-administration with efavirenz or fluconazole had a modest effect on azithromycin pharmacokinetics. However, nelfinavir significantly increased the Cmax and AUC of azithromycin. Despite this, no dosage adjustment of azithromycin is recommended when administered with these drugs. Nonclinical Toxicology: Carcinogenicity: Long-term animal studies to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of azithromycin have not been performed. Mutagenicity: Azithromycin has shown no mutagenic potential in standard laboratory tests, including the mouse lymphoma assay, human lymphocyte clastogenic assay, and mouse bone marrow clastogenic assay. Phospholipidosis: Intracellular phospholipid accumulation (phospholipidosis) has been observed in some tissues of mice, rats, and dogs given multiple doses of azithromycin. Affected tissues included the liver, gallbladder, kidney, spleen, pancreas, eye, and dorsal root ganglia. This effect was observed at doses similar to or lower than the highest recommended adult human dose when expressed on a body surface area basis. Phospholipidosis has been shown to be reversible after discontinuation of azithromycin treatment. Neonatal Rats: Phospholipidosis was also observed in neonatal rats dosed for 18 days at 30 mg/kg/day, which is less than the pediatric dose of 60 mg/kg based on surface area. The significance of these findings for animals and humans is unknown. This detailed explanation provides a comprehensive understanding of the pharmacokinetics, metabolism, elimination, and nonclinical toxicology of azithromycin, as well as its implications for specific patient populations and drug-drug interactions.
